title: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: a student's chant that asks for the body first, and asks Brahman not to let go

segments.voice: Then two weeks of the peace chants, day five. Yesterday, bhadram karnebhih: may we hear with our ears what is good, before any study begins. Today's chant goes one step further and asks for the ears themselves.

Exam week has its own diet: cold coffee, crackers, sleep in short pieces, the body treated like a phone that only has to last until tonight. Then there's the peace chant tradition sets with the Kena and the Chandogya, and it does two odd things. Before any study, it asks for the body. And halfway through, the student says to Brahman: never turn me away. Why would a student need to ask that?
screen: `COLD COFFEE, SHORT SLEEP.` → `IT ASKS FOR THE BODY FIRST.` → `NEVER TURN ME AWAY?`

segments.voice: The chant is known by its first words, apyayantu mamangani. In plain words, it begins: may my limbs grow strong. My speech, my breath, my eyes, my ears, my strength, and all my senses. Then the turn: all this is the Brahman of the Upanishads. And then the promise, both ways. May I never turn Brahman away. May Brahman never turn me away. Let there be no turning away. It ends by asking that the teachings found in the Upanishads live in the one who delights in the self. May they be in me. Then: Om, peace, peace, peace. The first puzzle solves itself once you see the line: all this is Brahman. The limbs, the breath, the ears are not obstacles to study. They are named as Brahman, so they're the first thing the student asks to have fed. Now the second. A student's chant might be expected to promise loyalty and stop there. Instead it asks from both sides: not only that the student hold on, but that Brahman not let go. Saha navavatu prayed that teacher and student not turn against each other. This chant hopes the same for the student and Brahman.
screen: `MAY MY LIMBS GROW STRONG.` · `ALL THIS IS BRAHMAN.` · `NO TURNING AWAY, BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `MAY THE TEACHINGS LIVE IN ME.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and stretch slowly: spread your fingers, roll your shoulders back, then let everything settle. Breathe into the parts the chant names, one at a time: the throat, the chest, the eyes, the ears. For the rest of the sit, treat the body as the first thing being fed, not the thing in the way.
The peace chants, and today apyayantu: may my limbs grow strong, and may I never turn Brahman away, nor Brahman me.
Pocket this: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad, strength first, and no turning away. See you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Apyayantu asks first that the limbs, breath, eyes and ears grow strong, and calls all this Brahman. Feeding the body is part of study.
